newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan surplus not set for drastic uptrend -- MITI.
newsitem.headline: Japan surplus not set for drastic uptrend -- MITI.

text.p: Japan's trade surplus is not heading towards a period of drastic expansion such as was seen in the years before 1993, Vice Trade Minister Osamu Watanabe told a news conference on Monday.
Watanabe said that although Japan's trade surplus was expanding and had risen sharply in April and May as well as July, the July increase was not as big as those for April and May.

He said the effects of the rise in the consumption tax in April were a major factor. "Looking over the period (April-July) as a whole, we can say July's figures also show that the effects of the consumption tax are gradually fading."
He added that structural changes such as the shift by manufacturers of production overseas and increased investment overseas meant the trade surplus was unlikely to expand at a drastic pace.
Asked about the trend of car exports, Watanabe said: "Looking at the big picture, Japanese carmakers are now moving towards increasing production from facilities abroad."

But he said domestic car sales for August were unlikely to show a large improvement from July. "July car sales recorded a disappointing fall of 10 percent. Unfortunately, preliminary data for August shows there will not be a large change."
But he added that car dealers expected replacement demand to emerge later on in the year.

Asked about recent criticism by U.S.Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky that Japan had fallen short of fulfilling an agreement to open its car market, and that the number of Japanese dealers signing up to sell cars made by the U.S. "Big Three" had fallen far short of expectations, Watanabe said: "It is up to U.S. carmakers to work hard and increase the number of dealers. It is unrelated to the Japanese government."
He added: "I expect U.S. carmakers to be bold and to get on with the business of selling."
He added that matters between the two governments had been settled with their 1995 car accord.
The Finance Ministry announced earlier on Monday that Japan's trade surplus rose for the fourth successive month in July, surging 69.7 percent from a year earlier to 849.08 billion yen.

The customs-cleared trade surplus with the United States, often a source of friction, jumped 35.7 percent in July from a year earlier to 420.55 billion yen. The figures were not adjusted for seasonal factors.
